Pricing per API call makes sense for infrastructure that's used in bursts, but I'd want to see the numbers before committing. A few hundred calls a day at $0.002 each is trivial, and the bill stays predictable. The trouble starts when one API request fans out into five or six internal calls, or when retries count as billable. Then the cost per user action can be several times what the pricing page suggests. I'd check whether they meter successful responses or every attempt, and whether there's a hard spending cap, because a runaway loop in someone's app can produce a surprise invoice overnight.

The other question is lock-in. Per-call pricing is easy to start with, but the moment you build your product around their response format, switching providers gets expensive. Their docs say the API is standard, but the edge cases (rate limit behavior, pagination quirks, how they handle partial failures) are where migrations actually hurt. If they publish a clear export path and their SDK is thin enough to replace, that lowers the risk a lot. If the SDK does a lot of hidden work, you're effectively paying for their abstractions along with their endpoints.

Still, I'd give them credit for not asking for a monthly commitment up front. Plenty of companies in this space require a contract before you can even see whether the API works for your use case. A pay-as-you-go model lets a small team test it on real traffic for the cost of a coffee. If the free tier is generous enough to run a real prototype and the metering is transparent, it's a reasonable bet. I'd just set a billing alert on day one and read the usage dashboard after the first week, since that's when you'll see whether the per-call estimate matches reality.

Interesting approach, but I'd want to see how it behaves under write contention before trusting it with anything important. Most new databases look great on single-node benchmarks, and the hard parts (replication lag, failover, what happens to in-flight transactions during a partition) usually show up later. Does the consistency model get documented clearly, or is it "eventually consistent with some caveats"? That distinction matters a lot for anyone choosing between this and Postgres.

The storage layer choices are the part I'd look at first. If it's an LSM-tree, compaction tuning will dominate tail latency under sustained writes. If it's B-tree based, you're trading write amplification for simpler read paths. Benchmarks that only show average throughput hide both of these, so p99 and p99.9 numbers under mixed workloads would be more useful to me than headline QPS.

That said, open-sourcing it early and being explicit about what it doesn't do yet is the right move. I'd rather see a project say "not production ready for multi-region writes" than a marketing page that implies it is. If the maintainers publish a Jepsen-style test report or a clear list of known anomalies, I'd become a much more willing early adopter.

Voice assistants have gotten noticeably worse, and it's not just nostalgia talking. A decade ago, asking Siri or Alexa to set a timer or check the weather usually worked on the first try. Now the same request often fails, gets routed to a web search, or triggers a canned "I'm not sure about that." The core tasks that justified buying these devices in the first place have become less reliable, even as the companies pitch them as AI platforms.

I suspect a big part of the problem is that the business model never supported the ambition. Amazon and Google spent years building voice assistants that were cheap to run and mostly drove shopping and ecosystem lock-in, so there was little incentive to make them great at open-ended conversation. When large language models arrived, the companies had to retrofit them onto old intent-matching pipelines, and the results have been uneven. Some features got more capable while basic commands broke in new ways, and the teams maintaining the old systems were often reassigned or cut.

The fix isn't obvious, but I'd like to see companies stop chasing demos and focus on reliability for the handful of tasks people actually use daily: timers, music, lights, reminders, and calls. Make those work every time, be honest when something isn't supported, and stop padding answers with ads or web results. A boring assistant that never misses a timer would be a far better product than a clever one that sometimes does.

Voice assistants got much worse over the last few years and nobody at the big companies seems to care. When I started using them they could set a timer, play a song, and tell me the weather. Now half the time it says "I'm sorry, I didn't quite get that" to a question it answered perfectly two months ago. I think the problem is that they moved everything to the LLM part and forgot the boring command parts still need to work. My guess is the old system had hard rules that always fired, and the new one guesses, so when the guess is wrong you just get nothing.

Code review slows teams down, but only in the way that brakes slow a car. Nobody measures a car's quality by its top speed, and a review queue that sits for three days is a real cost. The honest version of the argument is that review latency is a tax, and the question is whether what you buy with it is worth more than the time. On teams where reviews are a rubber stamp, it isn't. On teams where a reviewer catches a race condition or a permissions bug before it ships, it's the cheapest debugging you'll ever do.

I think most of the slowdown people complain about comes from how review is run, not from review itself. Large PRs get reviewed superficially because nobody has an hour to spare, small PRs get stuck because the reviewer is in meetings, and style debates eat attention that should go to design. Teams that keep reviews small, set an explicit expectation for first response within a few hours, and automate the formatting and lint arguments usually find that review adds little delay while keeping most of its value. Pairing or reviewing in real time can also cut the round trips that make async review feel slow.

The strongest counterpoint is that review can create a false sense of safety. Two people approving a change doesn't mean it's correct, and when reviewers know someone else will look, they may skim harder than they would alone. So I'd measure the outcome rather than the ritual. Track how often reviews catch real defects, how long changes wait, and how often bugs escape. If review is catching things, keep it and make it faster. If it's catching nothing but typos, cut it back and put the effort into tests and staged rollouts, which catch more problems per hour spent.

Location data brokers like this are a privacy problem that users can't fix by themselves. The "anonymized" label doesn't hold up. Researchers have repeatedly shown that a handful of timestamped points is enough to identify someone, since most people's daytime and nighttime locations are unique. A pin at a home address and a pin at a workplace identify a person, and the pins from a clinic or a place of worship reveal far more. Once that data is sold, the buyers include ad networks, insurers, data resellers, and anyone else willing to pay, and the people in the dataset never agreed to any of it. Most of them probably granted location permission to a weather or flashlight app and never imagined it would end up in a commercial feed.

The business model also means the incentives run the wrong way. Each new SDK bundled into an app adds another source of location pings, and the app developer collects revenue for each one. Opt-out toggles usually don't stop collection, and the data often persists long after the user deletes the app. Regulators have fined some of these companies, but the fines are small compared to the revenue, and the data that has already been resold can't be recalled. I'd like to see hard limits: no sale of precise location at all, mandatory deletion within a fixed window, and real liability when a broker's dataset gets used to track someone who has been stalked or targeted.

This is the third "free" app this month that turned out to be a location data pipeline with a flashlight icon on top. I don't need to know your location for a weather widget, and "we may share with partners" is doing a lot of work when the partners are data brokers who resell pings to anyone with a card. Did anyone actually read the privacy policy, or are we just going to keep installing these and acting surprised? I skimmed it on my phone while waiting for a bus, and even that was enough to see "precise geolocation" and "advertising partners" in the same paragraph.

The fix isn't complicated: deny location permission by default, use "while using" instead of "always," and kill the advertising ID. But almost nobody does this, and the app stores make it hard to tell what's collected. I've got to run, so I'll just say that if your app's entire business model depends on selling where people walk, it shouldn't be surprising when people stop trusting it.

Hi maintainers, thanks for building and sharing this tool. I'd like to ask for a way to turn off telemetry. An explicit opt-out, ideally both a config option and an environment variable, would make it much easier to adopt the tool in those settings and would make the data-handling behavior clearer to everyone.

Thanks for putting this together, and I agree with dropping Python 3.7 support. The version reached end-of-life in June 2023, so it no longer receives security patches, and maintaining compatibility with it adds friction to both the codebase and CI. Keeping the older interpreter in the test matrix consumes runner time and makes it harder to adopt newer language features and standard library improvements that would simplify our code.

Downstream users who are still on 3.7 can continue pinning to the last release that supported it, and the changelog can call out the change clearly so people can plan their upgrades. I'd suggest we also remove any 3.7-specific workarounds and update the `python_requires` metadata in the same PR so the change is enforced at install time. Happy to help with that cleanup if it's useful.

Title: Tips for Selling Handmade Candles Online? Here's What's Working for Me

Hi everyone,

I've been making soy candles at home for about two years, and I finally started selling them through my own online shop this spring. It's been a steep learning curve, so I wanted to share a few things that have helped.

First, photography matters more than you'd think. Natural light and a simple background made a huge difference in my sales. Second, be honest in your descriptions: burn times, wax type, and scent strength. Customers come back when they know what to expect. Third, test your candles before listing them. I burn every new batch for several hours to check for tunneling and even melt pools.

Shipping was my biggest headache. Glass jars break, and heat can warp candles in transit. Good padding and a note asking customers to avoid extreme temperatures have cut my damage claims a lot.

What selling strategies have worked for you? I'd love to hear your tips, especially on pricing and social media.

Hey everyone, first time posting here. I'm 35, I work in logistics, and about eight months ago I decided to learn to code. I kept waiting for the "right time," and then I realized that time was never going to show up on its own.

The first few weeks were humbling. I spent an entire evening trying to figure out why my variable wasn't printing, only to find I'd misspelled it. Younger classmates in my bootcamp-style course seemed to pick things up instantly, and I doubted myself constantly.

What helped was treating every bug as a normal part of the job rather than proof I didn't belong. I started keeping a notes file of mistakes and fixes, and I built small, ugly projects, like a script that sorts my shipping spreadsheets. It works, and it saves me about an hour a week.

**Title: Startup offer vs. bank offer, how would you decide?**

Hi all, I'm stuck between two offers and would appreciate outside perspective.

The first is a Series B startup with a product I believe in. The role is broad, I'd be working closely with the founders, and the equity could be meaningful if the company succeeds. The salary is a bit below market, and I know the runway is finite.

The second is a large bank in a well-established analytics division. The pay is higher, the benefits are excellent, and the work is stable. The downside is that the role is narrower, and I'm worried it could become a stepping stone that leads nowhere exciting.

I'm early in my career and want to optimize for learning and long-term options, not just the next paycheck. Some questions I'm wrestling with:

- How much weight should I give to equity I can't value precisely?
- Does startup experience usually carry more weight in future hiring than bank experience, or the reverse?
- How do you weigh financial security against growth?

I'd love to hear how others have approached a similar choice. Thanks in advance.

Slow Docker builds usually come down to a few common causes:

1. **Poor layer ordering.** If you `COPY . .` before installing dependencies, every source change invalidates the dependency cache. Copy manifest files first (`package.json`, `requirements.txt`, `go.mod`), install, then copy the rest.

2. **Large build context.** Docker sends everything in the directory to the daemon. Add a `.dockerignore` for `.git`, `node_modules`, build output, logs, and local virtualenvs.

3. **No cache reuse.** In CI, each build often starts cold. Use `--cache-from`, registry cache (`--cache-to type=registry`), or BuildKit cache mounts.

4. **Heavy base images.** Full OS images with build tools add time and size. Try slimmer variants like `-slim` or `-alpine`, though alpine can be slower for some compiled dependencies.

5. **Expensive package installs.** Use cache mounts for package managers:
   ```
   RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt
   ```

6. **Multi-stage builds.** Separate build and runtime stages so compilers and dev dependencies don't ship or rebuild unnecessarily.

7. **Emulation.** Building for another architecture (for example, arm64 on an amd64 host) uses QEMU and can be very slow. Build natively or use `buildx` with multiple nodes.

To diagnose, run `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build --progress=plain .` and see which step takes the most time. Share the Dockerfile and that output if you want more specific help.

The most common causes are unstable props, missing memoization, and state set too high in the tree. Start by confirming what's re-rendering with the React DevTools Profiler ("Highlight updates when components render" helps too).

Common fixes:

1. **Stop passing new objects/functions as props.** `style={{...}}`, inline arrow functions, and array literals create new references on every render. Move them out of the component, or wrap them in `useMemo` / `useCallback`.

2. **Wrap expensive children in `React.memo`.** This only helps if their props are stable, so fix step 1 first.

3. **Lift state down.** If a state change in a parent re-renders a large tree, move that state into a smaller child component.

4. **Use `children` as a slot.** Content passed as `children` doesn't re-render when a wrapper's own state changes.

5. **Split context.** A single context value that changes often re-renders every consumer. Separate frequently changing values from stable ones, and memoize the provider's `value`.

6. **Don't put derived data in state.** Compute it during render, or memoize it with `useMemo`, instead of storing it and syncing with `useEffect`.

7. **Check effect dependencies.** An object or array in a `useEffect` dependency list that's recreated each render can cause loops of updates.

8. **Avoid StrictMode confusion.** In development, StrictMode intentionally double-renders. Production behavior is what matters for performance.

Ran into this a lot. Usually it's one of three things:

1. **Parent state changes re-render everything below it.** Move the state down into the component that actually uses it, or pass the expensive child in as `children` so it doesn't re-render when the parent's state changes.

2. **Objects, arrays, and functions get recreated every render.** `{}`, `[]`, and inline arrow functions are new references each time, so any child wrapped in `React.memo` still sees "new" props. Wrap functions in `useCallback` and objects or arrays in `useMemo`, but only for the props that are actually passed to memoized children. Don't sprinkle them everywhere.

3. **Context is pushing updates to everyone.** Any component using `useContext` re-renders whenever the context value changes. If you're putting a fast-changing value in context, split it into smaller contexts or move it to something like Zustand or Jotai that lets components subscribe to slices.

To find the real culprit, install the React DevTools profiler, hit record, do the thing that's slow, and look at the "why did this render?" setting. It'll tell you which props or state changed, which is usually faster than guessing.

Also, don't memoize everything preemptively. `React.memo` and friends have their own cost, and a lot of re-renders are cheap. Only optimize what the profiler shows as slow.

Use URI-based major versions (`/v1/users`) for breaking changes, and avoid versioning anything else in the URL. Most of the work is in not breaking clients in the first place.

**Core rules:**
- **Only bump the major version for breaking changes**, such as removing fields, renaming things, changing types, or changing semantics. Adding optional fields or endpoints is non-breaking.
- **Keep old versions running** for a published deprecation window (often 6-12 months). Announce it early, send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers (RFC 8594), and track who still calls the old version.
- **Make clients tolerant.** Document that clients should ignore unknown fields and that enums may grow. This lets you ship many changes without a new version.

**Where to put the version:**
- **URI path** (`/v2/`) is the most common choice. It's explicit, easy to route, cacheable, and easy to debug.
- **Header or media type** (`Accept: application/vnd.acme.v2+json`) is more "pure REST," but harder for users and tooling.
- **Date-based versions** (Stripe-style, `Stripe-Version: 2026-11-18`) let you pin behavior per account and evolve gradually. They're great if you can afford the implementation cost.

**Practical tips:**
- Version the whole API, not individual endpoints, so mixing versions doesn't confuse people.
- Maintain an OpenAPI spec per version and generate changelogs from diffs.
- Consider running breaking changes behind a per-client opt-in before flipping the default.

Should Phones Be Banned in Schools?

Smartphones have become a constant presence in students' lives, and many schools have responded with strict rules that keep them out of classrooms. A full ban on phones in schools is a reasonable policy, because it protects learning, reduces distraction, and supports students' well-being.

The most important argument is focus. A phone on a desk, even when silent, pulls attention toward notifications, messages, and games. Research on "brain drain" suggests that the mere presence of a phone can reduce working memory and concentration. In a classroom where teachers are trying to explain fractions or analyze a poem, that lost attention adds up quickly. A ban removes the temptation entirely, so students can concentrate on the lesson instead of resisting the urge to check their screens.

A ban also addresses social and emotional concerns. Phones expose students to cyberbullying, group chats that continue into the school day, and social media comparisons that can damage self-esteem. Keeping phones out of the building during school hours gives students a daytime break from these pressures and encourages face-to-face interaction at lunch, between classes, and on the playground.

Critics argue that phones are useful tools and that a ban treats students as untrustworthy. They point to emergency communication, research apps, and calculators. These concerns are real, but they can be addressed without allowing phones throughout the day. Schools can provide landline access in offices for emergencies, supply school-owned devices for research, and store personal phones in lockers or pouches during class. A targeted policy keeps the benefits while avoiding the drawbacks.

Finally, a ban sends a clear message about the purpose of school. Education depends on sustained attention, careful thinking, and real relationships. When schools set firm boundaries around phones, they show students that learning deserves their full focus.

For these reasons, schools should ban phones during the school day. A well-designed policy protects students' attention, health, and relationships, and it gives them the best chance to learn.

Will Robots Take More Jobs Than They Create?

Every wave of automation has sparked the same fear: that machines will leave people without work. The steam engine, the assembly line, and the personal computer each displaced workers, yet each also produced new industries and occupations that earlier generations could not have imagined. Whether robots will take more jobs than they create depends on how quickly technology advances, how societies respond, and what kinds of work remain uniquely human.

The case for job loss is serious. Modern robots and artificial intelligence can perform routine physical and cognitive tasks, from assembling cars to processing insurance claims. Unlike earlier machines, which mainly extended human muscle, these systems can imitate some forms of judgment. Economists such as Daron Acemoglu have argued that automation can reduce demand for certain workers, especially those in middle-skill jobs, and can widen income inequality when the gains flow mainly to owners of capital. If technology spreads faster than workers can retrain, the losses could be concentrated and painful.

Still, history suggests that new work tends to follow new technology. Automation lowers costs, which increases demand for goods and services and creates jobs elsewhere in the economy. Entirely new fields, from software development to renewable energy maintenance, have emerged alongside automation. Many roles that require empathy, creativity, physical dexterity in unpredictable settings, or human trust, such as nursing, teaching, and skilled trades, are difficult to automate fully.

The outcome is not predetermined. Governments and employers can invest in education, apprenticeships, and lifelong learning to help workers move into emerging roles. Policies such as wage insurance, portable benefits, and fair distribution of productivity gains can cushion the transition. Without such efforts, robots could indeed eliminate more jobs than they create for many people, even if total employment eventually recovers.

In the end, robots will probably create many jobs while eliminating others. The more important question is whether the benefits are shared broadly. Technology itself does not decide who prospers; the choices made by societies do. Preparing people for change, rather than assuming it will sort itself out, is the surest way to ensure that automation expands opportunity instead of narrowing it.

Should Everyone Learn a Second Language?

Learning a second language is often treated as an optional hobby, something for people with a talent for languages or a reason to travel. Yet the case for requiring it of everyone is stronger than it first appears. A second language changes how people think, connects them to others, and prepares them for a world that is already multilingual.

The cognitive benefits are well documented. Bilingual people practice switching between systems of sound, grammar, and meaning, and that practice appears to strengthen attention and flexible thinking. Learning a language also teaches that the same idea can be expressed in more than one way, which is a lesson in humility. Grammar lessons reveal that English is not the default logic of human speech but one choice among many.

Language learning also builds empathy. Speaking someone's language, even imperfectly, signals respect and opens conversations that translation cannot fully reach. Anyone who has tried to order food or ask for directions in a foreign country knows the vulnerability and the gratitude that follow. Those experiences make people more patient with newcomers and more curious about neighbors who speak differently.

Practical arguments matter too. Many communities in the United States, Canada, and Europe are multilingual, and workplaces increasingly serve customers and colleagues across borders. A second language is a skill that employers value and that can make public services more accessible to everyone.

Critics argue that mandatory language study wastes time, since many students forget what they learn and few reach fluency in school. This objection is fair, but it points to poor teaching, not to a flaw in the goal. Programs that emphasize real conversation, immersion, and early start times produce better results. The answer is to teach languages well, not to abandon the effort.

Requiring a second language is not about turning everyone into a translator. It is about giving every person a window into another way of living and speaking. In a connected world, that window is worth opening for everyone.
